name: Furosemide
lead: Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a prescription loop diuretic used to treat oedema from heart failure, liver scarring (cirrhosis) and kidney disease, and sometimes high blood pressure.[1][12] It was patented in 1959 and approved for medical use in 1964, is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, and was the 29th most prescribed drug in the United States in 2023.[1]

Furosemide acts within about an hour by mouth and within minutes by injection, causing the kidney to excrete large amounts of sodium, chloride, potassium and water.[1] The US label carries a prominent warning that it is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion, and that careful medical supervision is required.[12]

In bodybuilding and physique communities furosemide is discussed as a way of dropping water weight, and it is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's banned list because it may mask other drugs.[1] No trial in the sources reviewed has examined it for cosmetic facial slimming or depuffing; its clinical evidence base concerns patients with fluid overload.

paras: Furosemide is mainly used for oedema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis and renal disease including nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension when thiazides are inadequate or kidney or heart impairment is present.[12][1] It is often viewed as first-line for oedema in heart failure.[1] It is also used in adjunct therapy for brain or lung oedema where rapid diuresis is needed, and for severe hypercalcaemia with rehydration.[1] In nephrotic syndrome and hypoalbuminaemia it is sometimes combined with albumin.[1][3]

Furosemide is used in horses to reduce exercise-induced pulmonary haemorrhage; its use is permitted in some US racing jurisdictions and prohibited in many other countries, and major US tracks ban its use on race days.[1]

Outside medicine, furosemide is discussed in physique contexts as a short-term way to shed water.[13] Any change in appearance reflects fluid loss rather than fat or bone change, and the label warns about the risk of excessive diuresis.[12]

Trials in acute decompensated heart failure have compared bolus and continuous infusion and low versus high doses of intravenous furosemide.[10] Combination strategies with thiazide diuretics, albumin and hypertonic saline have been tested to improve diuretic response.[9][3][4] The TRANSFORM-HF trial compared torsemide with furosemide after heart-failure hospitalisation and measured all-cause mortality.[5]

Common effects include orthostatic hypotension and lightheadedness, tinnitus and photosensitivity; serious effects include electrolyte abnormalities, low blood pressure and hearing loss.[1] Electrolyte disturbances can include hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia, and gout from hyperuricaemia and hyperglycaemia may occur.[1] Furosemide is associated with ototoxicity in post-marketing reports and observational studies, although age is a major confounding risk factor.[1] Long-term use in heart failure has been associated with thiamine deficiency.[1] It can cause kidney injury, usually by dehydration and usually reversible; sulfonamide allergy is a precaution.[1] In infants, furosemide use is associated with nephrocalcinosis.[6]

The label lists numerous gastrointestinal, hypersensitivity and other reactions, and it has been shown to cause unexplained maternal deaths and abortions in rabbits at multiples of the maximum human dose; no adequate studies exist in pregnant women.[12] Interactions include NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, antiarrhythmics and other diuretics.[1] The Wikipedia article and label both stress monitoring of electrolytes and renal function.

Furosemide inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, increasing urinary excretion of sodium, chloride and potassium and abolishing the corticomedullary osmotic gradient.[1] It is also a non-competitive blocker of certain GABA-A receptor subtypes in laboratory work.[1]

Oral bioavailability is about 47 to 70 percent, protein binding 91 to 99 percent, and about half is excreted unchanged in urine; the elimination half-life is about 2 hours and is prolonged in heart failure and severe kidney disease.[1] Efficacy depends on the concentration of drug in urine rather than plasma.[1]
Furosemide is prescription-only. WADA bans it because it may mask other substances.[1]

Mentions on T Nation are mostly from patients who take Lasix for heart or kidney problems and describe unpleasant side effects such as frequent urination; one user refers to bodybuilders who 'DNP and Lasix' their way to leanness.[13]
No studies found on furosemide for cosmetic facial slimming or depuffing in healthy people.

In patients, the large DOSE trial of 308 people with acute decompensated heart failure compared bolus versus infusion and low versus high dose intravenous furosemide.[10] A CLOROTIC trial tested adding hydrochlorothiazide to intravenous furosemide in acute heart failure, with co-primary endpoints of weight change and dyspnoea.[9] Meta-analyses examined furosemide with albumin and with hypertonic saline.[3][4] Randomized trials have also examined postpartum furosemide in preeclampsia and furosemide safety in preterm infants at risk for bronchopulmonary dysplasia.[7][8] A trial in people with chronic renal insufficiency compared saline, mannitol and furosemide for contrast-induced renal function decline.[11]

timeline.event: New York becomes the last US state to approve its use in racehorses.[1]
